Wednesday, September 23, 2026
Billing Insight Wednesday

Medicare Advantage denials often happen when a practice treats an MA plan like traditional Medicare.

MA plans may apply their own medical-necessity criteria, prior-authorization lists, step-therapy requirements, site-of-service rules, and notification standards. A notification is not always the same as authorization, and a requirement can vary by plan, service, setting, and member benefits.

Here’s how to fix it:

1. Capture the plan’s current requirements at scheduling, not from memory or a generic Medicare checklist.
2. Build a payer-specific requirement grid showing when authorization, notification, step therapy, or site-of-service review applies.
3. Record authorization numbers, approved services, units, dates, and effective periods in the patient account.
4. Track denials by MA plan and reason code to identify recurring medical-necessity or authorization gaps.
5. Reconcile payer policies quarterly and update scheduling, coding, and clinical review workflows.

The goal is simple: verify the right rule before care is delivered, document it clearly, and use denial data to prevent the next avoidable write-off.

🏥 Common Medical Billing Denial Codes

A denied claim is not the end of the billing process. It is an opportunity to identify the root cause, correct the issue, and prevent the same denial from happening again.

Here are some common Claim Adjustment Reason Codes (CARCs) that medical billing professionals should understand:

🔹 Patient Information Errors

CO-31: Patient cannot be identified as the insured
CO-9: Diagnosis is inconsistent with the patient's age
CO-16: Claim/service lacks information or has a billing error

🔹 Insurance Coverage Issues

CO-22: Care may be covered by another payer due to coordination of benefits
CO-26: Expenses incurred prior to coverage
CO-27: Expenses incurred after coverage terminated

🔹 Authorization & Referral Issues

CO-15: Authorization number is missing, invalid, or does not apply
CO-197: Precertification/authorization/notification was absent
CO-252: Required attachment or supporting documentation is missing

🔹 Medical Necessity & Coding Issues

CO-50: Services are not considered medically necessary by the payer
CO-11: Diagnosis is inconsistent with the procedure
CO-49: Service is non-covered because it is a routine/preventive or screening service

💡 The key to effective denial management is not simply reworking a denied claim — it's understanding WHY the claim was denied.

Accurate patient information, eligibility verification, authorization checks, proper coding, complete documentation, and timely follow-up can help reduce avoidable denials and improve the overall revenue cycle.

Know the code. Identify the cause. Fix the gap. Prevent the next denial.

Modifier GT is a telehealth billing modifier that indicates a service was delivered via interactive audio and video telecommunication systems (real‑time, synchronous). It is no longer required for most Medicare Part B professional claims but is still used in specific contexts like Critical Access Hospital (CAH) Method II institutional billing and by some Medicaid or commercial payers. 
📌 GT Modifier Overview
Definition: Identifies synchronous, real‑time telehealth services using both audio and video.
Type: HCPCS Level II modifier (not CPT).
Format: Appended to CPT/HCPCS codes (e.g., 99213‑GT, 90837‑GT).
Key Requirement: Must involve both audio and video — phone‑only calls or asynchronous transmissions do not qualify. 
🏥 Current Usage (2026)
Medicare Part B Professional Claims: GT retired in 2018; use modifier 95 with correct POS (02 or 10).
Critical Access Hospitals (CAH): GT still required under Method II institutional billing.
Medicaid & Commercial Payers: Some state Medicaid programs and legacy commercial payers still require GT — always verify payer policy.
Do Not Confuse With:
Modifier 95 → synchronous audio‑video (default for most payers).
Modifier 93 → audio‑only visits.
Modifier GQ → asynchronous store‑and‑forward. 
⚠️ Common Mistakes
Using GT by default → causes denials when payer requires 95.
Stacking GT and 95 → clearinghouses reject claims before payer review.
Applying GT to audio‑only calls → incorrect; use 93 instead.
Copying outdated cheat sheets → many still list GT as required for all Medicare telehealth claims, which is no longer true. 
✅ Best Practices for AR Teams
Verify payer rules before submitting — policies change frequently.
Check claim type (professional vs institutional).
Confirm technology used (audio‑video vs audio‑only).
Use correct POS codes (02 = telehealth, 10 = patient’s home).
Document clearly that service was synchronous audio‑video.
🔎 Quick Comparison
Modifier Use Case Medicare Status Risk if Misused
GT Synchronous audio‑video Retired for Part B; CAH institutional only Claim rejection/denial
95 Synchronous audio‑video Default for Medicare & most commercial None if documented
93 Audio‑only telehealth Accepted Denial if used for video
GQ Asynchronous telehealth Limited use Denial if used incorrectly
Would you like me to build a workflow chart showing when to apply GT vs 95 vs 93, so your AR team can quickly decide the correct modifier and avoid denials?
go moifier
Modifier GO is used in medical billing to indicate services delivered under a rehabilitative occupational therapy plan of care. It is one of the therapy modifiers that help payers distinguish between different types of therapy services.
📌 GO Modifier Overview
Definition: Occupational therapy services, delivered under an established plan of care.
Type: HCPCS Level II modifier.
Format: Appended to CPT/HCPCS codes (e.g., 97110‑GO, 97535‑GO).
Purpose: Ensures claims are correctly categorized as occupational therapy, separate from physical therapy (GP) or speech therapy (GN).
🏥 Therapy Modifier Set
GO → Occupational therapy.
GP → Physical therapy.
GN → Speech‑language pathology.
These modifiers are mandatory for Medicare and many commercial payers when billing therapy services.
⚠️ Common Mistakes
Using wrong therapy modifier → Denials occur if GP is used for OT services or vice versa.
Omitting therapy modifier → Claim rejected as incomplete.
Stacking multiple therapy modifiers → Only one therapy discipline modifier should be applied per service.
✅ Best Practices for AR Teams
Always confirm the discipline (OT, PT, SLP) before coding.
Append the correct therapy modifier to every therapy CPT code.
Ensure the plan of care is documented and signed by the provider.
Track therapy caps and thresholds (Medicare requires KX modifier once limits are exceeded).

Minimizing Claim Denials
• Pre-Submission Claim Scrubbing: Catch coding errors, modifier mismatches, missing information, and eligibility issues before the claim reaches the payer.
• Verify Patient Eligibility and Benefits: Confirm coverage, effective dates, deductibles, copays, prior authorization requirements, and network status before services are provided whenever possible.
• Use Specialized Coding Expertise: Although most Home Health and Hospice claims use the standard Medicare G codes, some insurances require other codes.
• Ensure Accurate CPT, ICD-10, and HCPCS Coding: Confirm that diagnosis and procedure codes accurately reflect the documentation and that the codes are appropriately linked.
• Check Modifier Accuracy: Review modifiers for proper use, sequencing, and payer-specific requirements. Incorrect or unnecessary modifiers are a common source of denials.
• Confirm Prior Authorizations and Referrals: Verify that required authorizations, referrals, and pre-certifications are obtained and documented before the service is performed.
• Submit Complete, Clean Claims: Ensure claims contain all required patient, provider, diagnosis, procedure, authorization, and supporting information before submission.
• Monitor Payer-Specific Rules: Keep up with changing payer policies, medical-necessity requirements, coding edits, filing deadlines, and claim-submission rules.
• Track Denial Patterns: Analyze denials by payer, provider, procedure, diagnosis, denial code, and root cause to identify recurring problems instead of treating every denial as an isolated event.
• Maintain Strong Documentation: Make sure clinical documentation supports the services billed, including medical necessity, procedures performed, units, time, and other payer-required details.
• Submit Claims Promptly: Establish processes that minimize delays between the date of service and claim submission, reducing the risk of timely-filing denials.
• Use Robust AR and Appeal Workflows: A low initial denial rate is important, but effective follow-up and appeals ultimately determine cash flow. Look for teams that investigate denials, write compelling appeal letters, submit supporting documentation, and pursue valid claims rather than automatically writing off low-dollar balances.
• Prioritize High-Value and Recoverable Denials: Use denial data to determine which accounts have the greatest financial impact and which denials have a strong likelihood of successful recovery.
• Work Denials Within Payer Deadlines: Track appeal and reconsideration deadlines so valid claims aren't lost simply because the follow-up occurred too late.
• Communicate With Clinical and Front-Office Teams: When a denial originates from registration, documentation, coding, authorization, or clinical workflow, communicate the root cause to the appropriate team so the same issue doesn't continue.
• Measure Denial Performance: Regularly monitor metrics such as initial denial rate, clean claim rate, denial overturn rate, days in AR, and dollars recovered through appeals.
• Continuously Improve the Billing Process: Use denial trends and payer feedback to update workflows, staff training, coding practices, and pre-submission checks.

Bottom Line
The best denial-reduction strategy isn't simply "submit fewer bad claims." It is a complete process that combines front-end eligibility and authorization checks, accurate specialty-specific coding, pre-submission claim scrubbing, strong documentation, and aggressive AR/appeal management. This helps prevent denials before submission while maximizing recovery when legitimate claims are denied.

⚠️ MODIFIER MISTAKES CAN DELAY YOUR PAYMENTS

A claim may contain the correct CPT code and diagnosis, yet still be denied or underpaid because of one incorrect, missing, or misplaced modifier.

Modifiers explain important details about a service, such as whether it was separate, significant, repeated, bilateral, or performed under special circumstances. When that information is inaccurate, the payer may request records, reject the claim, bundle services incorrectly, or delay reimbursement.

Here are four modifier mistakes healthcare practices should watch for:

✅ Missing Required Modifiers
Leaving out a payer-required modifier can make a valid service appear incomplete, bundled, or ineligible for separate payment.

✅ Using Modifier 25 Incorrectly
Modifier 25 should identify a significant, separately identifiable evaluation and management service performed on the same day as another procedure. The documentation must support work beyond what is normally included with that procedure.

✅ Modifier 59 Misuse
Modifier 59 indicates a distinct procedural service when appropriate. Using it without supporting documentation—or when a more specific X{EPSU} modifier is required—may trigger denials, audits, or payment reviews.

✅ Wrong Modifier Sequence
Modifier order can affect how a payer processes a claim. Placing pricing-related, payment-related, or informational modifiers in the wrong sequence may result in incorrect adjudication.

Before submitting a claim, your billing team should verify:

🔹 The modifier matches the service performed
🔹 The medical record supports its use
🔹 The payer’s current billing rules have been reviewed
🔹 Modifier order is correct
🔹 NCCI edits and bundling rules have been checked
🔹 The same modifier is not being applied automatically to every claim

Small coding details can have a major effect on cash flow. Strong claim reviews help reduce preventable denials, limit rework, and support more consistent reimbursement.

Correct diagnosis coding is the backbone of medical billing — it ensures the patient’s purpose of visit is captured, aligns CPT procedures with ICD‑10 diagnoses, and applies the right modifiers so Medicare and other payers reimburse at the maximum allowable rate. Even a small mismatch between DX, CPT, and modifiers can cause denials, downcoding, or audits.

🔑 Why Correct Diagnosis (DX) Matters
Purpose of Visit: The diagnosis code explains why the patient came to the doctor’s office. Without a valid DX, CPT services look medically unnecessary.

Medical Necessity: Medicare requires CPT procedures to be justified by ICD‑10 codes. If DX doesn’t support CPT, reimbursement is denied.

Audit Protection: Incorrect DX coding increases risk of RAC audits and payer recoupments.

⚙️ How DX, CPT, and Modifiers Work Together
DX Codes: Identify the patient’s condition (e.g., M54.5 – Low back pain).

CPT Codes: Describe the service performed (e.g., 97110 – Therapeutic exercises).

Modifiers: Add context (e.g., GP – therapy plan of care, 59 – distinct service).

👉 Example:

Patient visits for low back pain (DX: M54.5).

Provider performs therapeutic exercise (CPT: 97110).

Modifier GP is added to show therapy service under a physician’s plan.

Claim is accepted because DX supports CPT, and modifier clarifies billing.

💡 Why This Is Critical for Medicare
Clean Claim Rates: Accurate DX‑CPT linkage improves first‑pass acceptance, reducing AR days.

Maximum Reimbursement: Correct coding prevents underpayment (from downcoding) and avoids overpayment audits.

Denial Reduction: Coding errors (wrong DX, missing modifiers) cause 30%+ preventable denials.

📊 Medicare Solution for Providers
Coding Accuracy Programs: Medicare RCM partners run audits to ensure DX matches CPT.

Documentation Support: Coders train providers to document medical necessity clearly.

Denial Management: Automated workflows catch DX‑CPT mismatches before submission.

Revenue Protection: Ensures providers get paid fairly, without compliance risks.

🚨 Risks of Wrong Coding
Claim Denials: Missing DX or incorrect modifier.

Delayed Payments: Downcoded claims reduce revenue.

Audit Exposure: High error rates (>10%) trigger Medicare RAC reviews.

✅ In short: Always analyze the patient’s purpose of visit, select the correct ICD‑10 DX, align it with CPT services, and apply the right modifiers. Medicare solutions that integrate coding audits, denial prevention, and documentation training help providers secure maximum reimbursement while staying compliant.

🧩 Coding Tip: Modifiers Matter!

Using the correct CPT modifiers is essential for accurate medical coding and clean claim submission. Always ensure modifiers are supported by proper documentation and applicable to the service.

Incorrect or missing modifiers can lead to claim denials, payment delays, and lost revenue.

✅ Right Code. Right Modifier. Right Claim.
